title: Ventilator alarm
banner: DRAFT, NOT clinically reviewed. Fictional scenario specification; never imported, published or shown to learners.
learning_objectives: Respond to a ventilator alarm by going to the patient first.
Secure ventilation before troubleshooting the machine.
Recognise that alarm limits and modes are changed only with authority.

sources.use: manufacturer manual: alarm and alternative ventilation statements for that device only
AARC issue paper, alarm management and backup ventilation sections: individualized settings, manufacturer-specific competence, communication

required_sources: Unit ventilator alarm policy, current manufacturer instructions and device-specific emergency competency verification
gaps: No published clinical scenario may exist until the review phase: this is a specification only.
The branching content, consequences and scoring are the author's reading of the cited sources and have had no clinical review.
Device-specific alarm behaviour differs by manufacturer and software; the scenario uses generic wording.

Cross-manufacturer principles are supported by the AARC safety issue paper; alarm causes and model-specific operating procedures still require trained local assessment. AACN's 2018 alert concerns ECG and pulse oximetry, not a ventilator operating standard.

Generic ventilator alarm wording and alternative ventilation steps require local respiratory therapist/manufacturer sign-off; this fictional exercise does not prescribe alarm limits or device operation.
permissions: Cited sources are paraphrased only; see the licensing register for each source's reproduction status.
setting: A fictional ventilated adult on a fictional unit; the ventilator is a generic device.

steps.info: A ventilated adult develops repeated high-airway-pressure alarms after repositioning. The patient is coughing and distressed. Earlier chest movement and oxygenation were satisfactory, but current effective ventilation has not been established.
steps.prompt: What should the nurse do before attempting to change alarm limits or ventilator settings?

options.text: Go to the patient and look at the patient, the airway, the circuit and the machine.
options.feedback: Going to the patient is the expected response to every alarm, and the machine's message guides but does not replace looking at the patient. High pressure may reflect airway resistance, coughing, dyssynchrony or reduced respiratory-system compliance; the alarm alone does not diagnose the cause. Avoid empirical sedation or setting changes before appropriate assessment.
options.consequence: Direct assessment may identify a correctable airway or circuit issue while clarifying whether emergency ventilation support is needed.

options.text: Silence the alarm and finish the task you were doing.
options.feedback: A temporary audible pause does not correct the underlying problem; remain with the patient and resolve or escalate the alarm. Muting behavior varies by device and alarm priority.
options.consequence: An alarm pause could conceal persistent ventilation difficulty and delay rescue.

options.text: Widen the alarm limits so the alarm stops.
options.feedback: Alarm limits and modes are changed only when authorised by order, protocol and training; extreme limits make alarms useless.
options.consequence: Wider limits could suppress an important warning without correcting its cause.

steps.info: At the next shared checkpoint, saturation is lower and chest movement remains poor. The high-pressure alarm persists. An immediately correctable cause has not been established; ventilation may be inadequate.
steps.prompt: What is the immediate priority when troubleshooting has not restored effective ventilation?

options.text: Call for skilled help and use the unit's approved emergency ventilation approach to ensure effective ventilation while the cause is addressed.
options.feedback: Inadequate ventilation or rapidly worsening oxygenation calls for immediate rescue with a trained team. Assess the airway and patient, call for help, and provide alternative ventilation by the unit's protocol if required rather than leaving the patient unsupported while troubleshooting. AARC endorses direct patient–ventilator assessment; specific emergency-device steps come from the unit and manufacturer. Facilities should have a backup ventilation plan and staff trained on the installed model. Activate the emergency pathway promptly; no particular circuit-disconnection or device maneuver is implied.
options.consequence: Skilled emergency assistance and the approved backup ventilation approach may restore support while the cause is investigated.

options.text: Keep troubleshooting the machine on your own.
options.feedback: Continuing to troubleshoot alone while ventilation is inadequate can delay rescue; call for skilled help and follow the emergency ventilation pathway.
options.consequence: Prolonged troubleshooting without rescue support could worsen hypoxaemia or delay emergency care.

options.text: Change the ventilator mode yourself to see if the patient improves.
options.feedback: Unsupervised ventilator changes do not substitute for urgent assessment and effective ventilation; use the unit's authorized emergency process.
options.consequence: An unauthorized mode change could worsen ventilation and complicate assessment.

steps.info: At the final shared checkpoint, the trained team has addressed an airway or circuit problem. Chest movement is equal, saturation has improved and the alarm is no longer active. Delivered support and alarm settings still need confirmation.
steps.prompt: What should the nurse verify and document before considering the episode resolved?

options.text: Confirm effective ventilation and reassess delivered volumes, pressures, oxygenation, airway and circuit with the trained respiratory team; document the event, response and ongoing monitoring plan in handover.
options.feedback: AARC 2024 supports direct bedside assessment and review of delivered tidal volume, plateau pressure and PEEP, including intrinsic PEEP when relevant. Check recovery with the trained team rather than treating the absence of an alarm as proof of adequate ventilation. Document and hand over the event. Confirm that alarm limits remain appropriate for the patient's prescribed support, and record changes and response with the team.
options.consequence: A documented recovery assessment and monitoring plan may help the next team recognize recurrence and verify prescribed support.

options.text: Document only that the alarm sounded.
options.feedback: An incomplete record loses the cause, the actions and the outcome.
options.consequence: An alarm-only note could omit the cause, response and remaining concerns.

options.text: Reset the alarm limits to the narrowest settings so any change will alarm.
options.feedback: Limits are set by order or protocol, not by the nurse's own choice.
options.consequence: Unnecessarily narrow limits could generate nuisance alarms and distract from meaningful changes.

learning_points: Every alarm is answered at the patient first.
If ventilation is inadequate and not rapidly correctable, call for skilled help and secure effective alternative ventilation as trained and directed by the local emergency pathway.
Do not silence alarms as a response or change limits and modes without authority.
After rescue, verify effective ventilation and review delivered volumes, airway pressures and PEEP with the respiratory team; document and hand over the event.
